title: Sleep Health & Lifestyle Analysis
text:
Methodology
This analysis employs a rigorous data science pipeline to handle non-normal distributions and small sample sizes effectively.

1. Data Processing
Missing values were handled, and feature engineering was performed (e.g., splitting blood pressure). Crucially, the Yeo-Johnson transformation was applied to normalize skewed predictors like physical_activity_level, ensuring the validity of linear assumptions.


2. Regression (Sleep Duration)
I compared a baseline Linear Regression (R2 =0.870) against Elastic Net Regression tuned via 10-fold Cross-Validation. Elastic Net successfully reduced RMSE to 0.285, demonstrating that regularization improved generalization on this dataset.


3. Classification (Sleep Quality)
To classify sleep as adequate or inadequate, I deployed a Random Forest Classifier against a Logistic Regression baseline. The Random Forest model achieved ~99% accuracy and an ROC AUC of 1.00, identifying stress_Level as a critical determinant.

Data Loading and Corpus Construction
The following code locates and collects all UN General Assembly speech text files by iterating over a session-based folder structure, where TXT directory contains subfolders (e.g. Session 01 - 1946), each of which stores individual speech text files (e.g. ARG_01_1946.txt).


Code
base_path <- "data/TXT"

session_dirs <- list.dirs(
  path = base_path,
  recursive = FALSE,
  full.names = TRUE
)

length(session_dirs)


[1] 79


Code
head(session_dirs)

[3] "data/TXT/Session 03 - 1948" "data/TXT/Session 04 - 1949"
[5] "data/TXT/Session 05 - 1950" "data/TXT/Session 06 - 1951"


Code
txt_files <- unlist(
  lapply(session_dirs, function(d) {
    list.files(
      path = d,
      pattern = "\\.txt$",
      full.names = TRUE
    )
  })
)

[1] 10952

The result of the length() checks shows that 79 session directories are detected, corresponding exactly to the 79 General Assembly years from 1946 to 2024. In addition, a total of 10,952 speech text files are collected. This is fully consistent with the dataset description, which reports 10,952 speeches from 202 countries, confirming that all expected speech files are correctly identified.


Code
speech_df <- tibble(
  file_path = txt_files,

glimpse(speech_df)

Each speech text file is read and combined into a tidy data frame, where each row corresponds to a single UN General Assembly speech. The output of glimpse() confirms that the data frame contains 10,952 rows and two columns (file_path and text).

speech_df <- speech_df %>%

title: DS202A - W11+1 Summative
text:
Exploratory Analysis of the Corpus
This part provides a descriptive overview of the UN General Debate corpus, focusing on variation in document length and lexical diversity across speeches. These patterns establish important baselines and motivate subsequent similarity and anomaly analyses by highlighting sources of heterogeneity that may influence textual comparisons.


Code
doc_stats <- summary(corp_un, n = ndoc(corp_un))

doc_stats <- doc_stats %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(
    document = Text,
    tokens = Tokens,
    types = Types,
    sentences = Sentences
  )

glimpse(doc_stats)


Rows: 10,952
Columns: 4
$ document  <chr> "text1", "text2", "text3", "text4", "text5", "text6", "text7…
$ tokens    <int> 3732, 4893, 2744, 3347, 1687, 1644, 1644, 1501, 3214, 4194, …
$ types     <int> 1111, 1105, 798, 937, 598, 568, 555, 596, 946, 1172, 549, 30…
$ sentences <int> 126, 125, 98, 98, 55, 53, 54, 46, 95, 109, 64, 24, 26, 73, 1…


The corpus summary is converted into a tidy data frame containing basic document-level statistics for all speeches, including the number of tokens, unique word types, and sentences.


Code
ggplot(doc_stats, aes(x = tokens)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#4C72B0", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Right-Skewed Distribution of UN General Debate Speech Lengths",
    x = "Number of tokens",
    y = "Number of speeches"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Document length exhibits a pronounced right-skew, with most speeches clustered at moderate lengths and a small number of extremely long outliers.


Code
ggplot(doc_stats, aes(x = sentences, y = tokens)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Sentence Count Strongly Predicts Speech Length, with a Small Set of Extreme Outliers",
    x = "Number of sentences",
    y = "Number of tokens"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









sentences and tokens are strongly correlated, but a small number of speeches deviate substantially from the main cluster. These extreme cases suggest candidates for anomalous speeches driven by exceptional verbosity.


Code
doc_stats_year <- doc_stats %>%
  mutate(
    year = docvars(corp_un, "year")
  )

yearly_tokens <- doc_stats_year %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_tokens = mean(tokens),
    median_tokens = median(tokens),
    n_speeches = n()
  )

The document-level statistics are then aggregated by year to compute average and median speech length, along with the number of speeches delivered each year. This yearly summary enables examination of temporal trends in speech length across the General Assembly.

  geom_line(color = "#C44E52") +

The average length of UN General Assembly speeches rises sharply from the late 1940s to around 1960, where it reaches a clear peak, before stabilizing and then gradually declining from the late 1980s onward. This pronounced early increase and peak indicate that speech length varies substantially across historical periods.


Code

  mutate(
    ttr = types / tokens

glimpse(doc_stats_year)

Columns: 6
$ document  <chr> "text1", "text2", "text3", "text4", "text5", "text6", "text7…

$ ttr       <dbl> 0.2976956, 0.2258328, 0.2908163, 0.2799522, 0.3544754, 0.345…


Type–Token Ratio (TTR) is computed for each speech as the ratio of types to tokens, providing a simple measure of lexical diversity that is less directly tied to document length than raw token counts. By associating ttr with year, this representation allows exploration of how lexical diversity varies across speeches and over time.


Code
ggplot(doc_stats_year, aes(x = ttr)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Type–Token Ratio Is Approximately Bell-Shaped",
    x = "Type–Token Ratio",
    y = "Number of speeches"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Code
ttr_by_year <- doc_stats_year %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_ttr = mean(ttr, na.rm = TRUE)
  )


The distribution of ttr is approximately bell-shaped, with most speeches concentrated within a relatively narrow range of lexical diversity. This suggests that while speech length varies substantially, the overall richness of vocabulary used in UN General Debate speeches is more stable.


Code
ggplot(ttr_by_year, aes(x = year, y = avg_ttr)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkred") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Lexical Diversity Declines Until the 1960s, Then Rises Gradually Thereafter",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average TTR"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Notably, the trough in average ttr around 1960 aligns with the peak in average document length observed earlier. This pattern is likely driven by length effects rather than substantive changes in vocabulary usage, highlighting the importance of interpreting lexical diversity measures jointly with document length.


Code
doc_stats_country <- doc_stats_year %>%
  mutate(
    country = docvars(corp_un, "country")
  )

top_countries <- doc_stats_country %>%
  count(country, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  pull(country)

country_tokens <- doc_stats_country %>%
  filter(country %in% top_countries) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(avg_tokens = mean(tokens))

ggplot(country_tokens, aes(x = reorder(country, avg_tokens), y = avg_tokens)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#8172B2") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Average UN General Debate Speech Length Varies Widely Across Countries",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Average number of tokens"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









The figure shows substantial cross-country variation in average speech length. Countries such as India and the United States tend to deliver longer speeches on average, while others cluster at lower token counts. These differences may reflect institutional speaking styles, and this heterogeneity motivates explicitly examining country-level patterns in subsequent analyses.

title: DS202A - W11+1 Summative
text:
Document Similarity Analysis


Code
set.seed(123)
sample_idx <- sample(seq_len(ndoc(corp_un)), 500)
corp_sim <- corp_un[sample_idx]


Because pairwise similarity computation scales quadratically with the number of documents, computing cosine similarity on the full corpus of over 10,000 speeches would be computationally infeasible. To address this, a random set of 500 speeches was selected from the full corpus, and similarity analysis was conducted on the resulting sub-corpus (corp_sim).






Why random sampling



Random sampling was adopted because it minimises prior assumptions in an exploratory similarity analysis where temporal and national structure are objects of investigation rather than design features.




Code
toks <- tokens(
  corp_sim,
  remove_punct = TRUE,
  remove_numbers = TRUE
) %>%
  tokens_tolower() %>%
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en"))

  margin = "documents",

title: DS202A - W11+1 Summative
text:
Discussion
Part A used similarity and anomaly perspectives to characterise both typical and exceptional patterns in UN General Debate speeches. Rather than treating these as separate exercises, the analysis shows that each perspective captures a distinct but complementary dimension of diplomatic discourse.
Similarity analysis reveals that national continuity is the primary source of textual alignment. Speeches by the same country remain lexically close across years, indicating stable rhetorical identities that outweigh shared temporal context. High similarity is driven by repeated, country-specific and policy-relevant language rather than generic diplomatic formulas.
By contrast, anomaly detection highlights moments of deviation that are not visible from similarity alone. Structural anomalies reflect historically specific periods of heightened verbosity, while semantic and contextual anomalies capture speeches that diverge from contemporaneous or national discourse despite being structurally typical. The limited overlap between anomaly types demonstrates that deviation is multidimensional.
Taken together, these findings suggest that UN General Debate discourse is simultaneously conservative and adaptive. National rhetorical styles exhibit strong continuity, yet departures emerge along multiple dimensions depending on historical context and reference frame. This underscores the value of combining similarity-based and anomaly-based approaches.

title: DS202A - W11+1 Summative
text:
Research Question and Motivation
The UN General Debate provides a record of how states publicly frame global issues in a multilateral forum. Since each speech reflects national priorities, taken together, they reveal how the international agenda has evolved over time.
This study asks:

How have the dominant thematic frames of UN General Debate speeches changed across decades, and to what extent do these shifts differ across countries?

The focus is on long-run patterns in thematic composition. To address this question, the analysis relies on unsupervised learning methods that allow thematic structures to emerge inductively from the data.






Why Unsupervised Learning



Supervised learning would require historically stable labels for speech themes, which are unavailable for UN General Debate speeches spanning nearly eight decades and would risk anachronistic interpretations. Unsupervised learning instead allows latent thematic structure to emerge from word co-occurrence patterns, enabling analysis of long-run changes in the semantic organisation of multilateral discourse.

title: DS202A - W11+1 Summative
text:
Limitations and Ethical Considerations
The findings presented here should be interpreted in light of several methodological and ethical constraints inherent in the analytical design.
From a methodological standpoint, the decade-level sampling and aggregation strategy necessarily smooths over within-decade variation and may obscure short-term rhetorical shifts linked to specific geopolitical events. Topic modeling outcomes are also sensitive to preprocessing decisions and to the number of topics specified, meaning that alternative specifications could yield somewhat different thematic delineations. Moreover, aggregation at the country–decade level abstracts from leadership turnover and internal political change, so the analysis captures dominant discursive orientations rather than the full heterogeneity of national speechmaking.
Ethical and interpretive considerations call for caution. Because topic modeling and clustering are inductive, topic labels and cluster interpretations necessarily reflect researcher judgment and should not be read as fixed national characteristics. The analysis is therefore descriptive rather than evaluative. More broadly, clustering functions as a heuristic tool, and uncritical interpretation risks reinforcing essentialised or stereotypical readings of national discourse, underscoring the need for careful contextualisation.

title: DS202A - W11+1 Summative
section: Conclusion: Long-Run Thematic Shifts and Cross-National Variation in UN Discourse
text:
Conclusion: Long-Run Thematic Shifts and Cross-National Variation in UN Discourse
This study examined how the thematic composition of UN General Debate speeches has evolved over time and how these changes vary across countries. Using unsupervised learning methods, the analysis combined topic modeling, dimensionality reduction, and clustering to trace long-run patterns in multilateral discourse while accounting for cross-national heterogeneity.
The results point to a clear reorientation of the international agenda. Early decades are dominated by multilateral institutions, Cold War rivalry, and security concerns, whereas later periods increasingly foreground development, governance, and sustainability. PCA-based analyses show that this shift follows a gradual and cumulative trajectory rather than abrupt breaks, with mid-period peaks reflecting the salience of decolonisation and regional conflict.
At the same time, the country–decade analysis demonstrates that states do not move uniformly through thematic space. While temporal dynamics structure the overall pattern, hierarchical clustering reveals recurring thematic configurations and notable country-specific deviations. These findings suggest that enduring national orientations and geopolitical constraints mediate how countries engage with evolving global priorities.
Taken together, the analysis shows that changes in UN General Debate discourse reflect both systemic temporal shifts and persistent cross-national differences. Unsupervised learning provides a coherent framework for capturing this dual structure, offering insight into how the international agenda evolves while remaining unevenly articulated across states.

Methodology
This analysis employs a two-step statistical approach to understand and predict customer churn.

title: Marketing Science: Multinomial Logit & Latent Class Analysis
text:
Methodology
This analysis moves beyond aggregate preferences by employing Latent Class Analysis (LCA) to uncover hidden segments within the consumer population.

1. Baseline Modeling (Multinomial Logit)
Initially, a standard Multinomial Logit (MNL) model was fitted to establish baseline average effects.
Result: Price has a significant negative effect (-0.37), and feature ads have a positive effect (+0.49) on brand choice across the aggregate population.


2. Identifying Heterogeneity (LCA)
To capture market heterogeneity, I fitted Finite Mixture Models using the flexmix package, testing from k=1 to k=6 classes.
Model Selection: Based on the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and model interpretability, a 4-class model was selected.

The summary statistics reveal that 23 customers remained active throughout the observation period. Out of the total 1,000 customers, 977 churn events were observed, ranging from day 3 to day 54. The median survival time was identified as 31 days, indicating a concentration of customer attrition around this point.
Furthermore, the data was stratified by Direct Mail (DM) reception status to visualize the distribution via a boxplot. The analysis indicates that the group receiving DM exhibits slightly higher median and quartile values compared to the non-recipient group. This observation suggests that receiving DM may be associated with prolonged customer retention.



The Cox proportional hazards model (PHM) is utilized to quantify the relationship between the reception of Direct Mail (DM) and customer churn duration.


Code
fit_DM <- flexsurvreg(
  Surv(Duration, Event) ~ DM,
  data = data_chap09_churn,
  dist = "weibullPH"
)

coef_tbl_DM <- as.data.frame(fit_DM$res) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("variable") %>%
  filter(variable %in% names(coef(fit_DM)))

coef_tbl_DM <- coef_tbl_DM %>%
  mutate(
    HR = exp(est),
    HR_se = HR*se,
    HR_L95 = exp(est - 1.96 * se),
    HR_U95 = exp(est + 1.96 * se)
  ) %>%
  select(variable, coef = est, se.coef=se, HR, HR_se, HR_L95, HR_U95)
print(coef_tbl_DM, digits = 3)


  variable      coef  se.coef     HR    HR_se HR_L95 HR_U95

2    scale  2.24e-05 6.45e-06  1.000 6.45e-06  1.000  1.000
3       DM -1.97e-01 6.41e-02  0.821 5.26e-02  0.724  0.931


The results indicate that the Hazard Ratio for DM recipients is 0.821 (95% CI: 0.724–0.931). Since the 95% confidence interval excludes 1, a statistically significant effect is observed. This estimate implies that the instantaneous risk of churn for customers who received DM is approximately 18% lower than for those who did not, assuming other conditions remain constant.


Code
plot(fit_DM, type = "hazard", ci = TRUE,
     newdata = data.frame(DM = 1),
     col = "blue", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Duration", ylab = "Hazard",
     main = "")

     newdata = data.frame(DM = 0),
     col = "red", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)
legend("topleft", legend = c("DM", "no DM"),
       col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2)









The figure above illustrates the estimated hazard functions stratified by the status of DM reception. The hazard for customers who received DM is observed to be consistently lower than that for customers who did not receive DM across the entire timeline.
Notably, the divergence between the two groups widens progressively during the latter half of the observation period (after day 30). This trend suggests that the receipt of DM exerts a suppressive effect on the risk of churn. Furthermore, the distinct separation of the 95% confidence intervals indicates that the difference between the two hazard functions is statistically significant.


Code

     newdata = data.frame(DM = 1), col = "blue")
plot(fit_DM, type = "survival", ci = TRUE,
     newdata = data.frame(DM = 0), col = "red", add = TRUE)

legend("bottomleft", c("DM", "No DM"), lwd = 1, col = c("blue","red"))









This figure depicts the estimated survival functions stratified by the presence or absence of DM reception. The survival probability for DM recipients remains consistently higher than that for non-recipients, indicating that customers who received DM exhibit a stronger tendency for prolonged service retention.
A marked divergence between the two groups becomes particularly apparent around the 30 to 40-day interval, suggesting that DM reception contributes to the mitigation of customer churn. Furthermore, the limited overlap between the 95% confidence intervals supports the conclusion that the observed difference in survival probabilities is statistically significant.




In the following code, a proportional hazards model based on the Weibull distribution is estimated, utilizing customer demographic attributes (Sex, Age) and behavioral characteristics (Freq, Amount) as explanatory variables. Subsequent to the model estimation, the influence of varying levels of variables that exhibited particularly significant hazard ratios on the survival and hazard functions is visualized.


Code
fit_full <- flexsurvreg(
  Surv(Duration, Event) ~  Sex + Age + Freq + Amount,
  data = data_chap09_churn,
  dist = "weibullPH"
)

coef_tbl_full <- as.data.frame(fit_full$res) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("variable") %>%
  filter(variable %in% names(coef(fit_full)))
coef_tbl_full <- coef_tbl_full %>%
  mutate(
    HR = exp(est),
    HR_se = HR*se,
    HR_L95 = exp(est - 1.96 * se),
    HR_U95 = exp(est + 1.96 * se)
  ) %>%
  select(variable, coef = est, se.coef=se, HR, HR_se, HR_L95, HR_U95)
print(coef_tbl_full, digits = 3)


  variable      coef  se.coef     HR    HR_se HR_L95 HR_U95

Both age(Age) and purchase frequency(Freq) were identified as statistically significant factors influencing churn risk. Specifically, the Hazard Ratio (HR) for Age was estimated at 0.976 (95% CI: 0.972–0.980), implying that each additional year of age corresponds to an approximate 2.4% reduction in the instantaneous risk of churn. Similarly, the HR for Freq was calculated as 0.857 (95% CI: 0.814–0.903), indicating that a single unit increase in purchase frequency is associated with a 14.3% decrease in churn risk. Since the 95% confidence intervals for both variables exclude the null value of 1, these effects are confirmed to be statistically significant. Conversely, the HR for gender(Sex) was 0.951 (95% CI: 0.833–1.085), and for purchase amount(Amount) was 0.917 (95% CI: 0.733–1.147). As these intervals encompass 1, no statistically significant impact was observed for these variables, suggesting that their influence on customer churn is limited within the context of this model.

1.3 Calculation Methods for Reliability and Validity Metrics
To facilitate the subsequent computation of Cronbach’s alpha, Composite Reliability (CR), and Average Variance Extracted (AVE), the necessary functions are defined in advance.


Code
alpha.coef <- function(x){
  z <- (ncol(x) / (ncol(x) - 1)) * 
    (1 - sum(diag(var(x))) / var(rowSums(x)))
  return(z)
}

cr_ave <- function(Flab, StdEst){
  FL <- StdEst[(StdEst["lhs"] == Flab) & (StdEst["op"] == "=~"),3]　
  FLlist <- colSums(apply(StdEst["rhs"], 1, 
                          function(x,fl){x==fl},FL)) > 0
  Lm <- StdEst[FLlist & (StdEst["op"] == "=~"), 4]
  e <-  StdEst[FLlist & (StdEst["op"] == "~~"), 4]
  
  CR <- sum(Lm)^2 / (sum(Lm)^2 + sum(e))
  AVE <- sum(Lm^2) / (sum(Lm^2) + sum(e))
  return(c(CR,AVE))
}

title: Text Mining UN General Debates (1946-2024)
text:
Methodology
By combining unsupervised learning with dimensionality reduction, this analysis uncovers macro-level trends in diplomatic history.

1. Corpus Analysis & Anomaly Detection
Using TF-IDF weighting and Cosine Similarity on a corpus of 10,952 speeches, I detected “Structural Anomalies” (e.g., historical verbosity peaks around 1960) and “Semantic Anomalies” where specific speeches significantly diverged from established national rhetorical styles.


2. Topic Modeling (LDA)
I applied Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) with Gibbs sampling (k=8) to identify latent themes. The model successfully distinguished between historical topics like Decolonization/Apartheid and contemporary issues such as Climate Change/Sustainable Development.


3. Dimensionality Reduction (PCA)
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was applied to the topic proportions to visualize temporal trajectories: - PC1: Illustrated a shift from “Security & Institutions” to “Governance & Sustainability”. - PC2: Captured the rise and fall of “Geopolitical Conflict,” peaking during the Cold War era (1970s/80s).

Distribution of Numeric Predictors
To ensure the reliability of regression models (Part 2), it is important to check the distribution of the numeric predictors. Models like linear and regularized regression perform optimally when predictors are (approximately) normally distributed. The following histograms visualize the distribution of each numeric variable cleaned in Q2.1 (excluding sleep_duration itself).


Code

  select(where(is.numeric), -sleep_duration)

numeric_predictors |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    title = "Distributions of Numeric Predictors",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Count"

The histograms reveal that several key predictors are not normally distributed, which could impact regression performance. While quality_of_sleep exhibits a clear left-skew, other important predictors like physical_activity_level and daily_steps do not show a simple, smooth skew. Instead, their distributions are visibly multi-modal, with data clustered around a few distinct peaks (e.g., 30, 45, 60 minutes of activity, or 5000, 8000 steps), suggesting they behave more like discrete or ordinal variables. This discrete and non-bell-shaped nature of the predictors can violate the assumptions of linear-based models like Elastic Net. Therefore, in the Part 2 modeling recipe, applying a transformation like the Yeo-Johnson transformation will be considered as a critical strategy to help normalize these distributions and improve potential model performance.






A Methodological Note on Data Leakage



Ideally, these predictor distributions would be assessed only on the train_data after splitting to prevent any data leakage. However, given the small sample size (n=374), the full dataset was used for this initial EDA to gain a more stable understanding of the underlying distributions. This knowledge is crucial for informing the modeling approach (e.g., the need for step_YeoJohnson), representing a pragmatic tradeoff. The transformation parameters themselves will, of course, be learned only from the train_data during the prep() step in Part 2.

text:
Q2.2 Fitting a baseline linear regression model
The next step is to fit the baseline linear regression model. This serves as a reference point for performance and is typically constructed by including all available predictors. A tidymodels workflow is established for this purpose. First, a linear_reg() specification is defined using the “lm” engine. A corresponding recipe is created, using the formula sleep_duration ~ . to designate sleep_duration as the outcome and all other variables as predictors. Within this recipe, step_rm(age_group) is used to prevent multicollinearity with the age variable, and step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) is applied to convert all factor variables into binary indicators for the regression. This model and recipe are bundled into a workflow and then fitted to the train_data to create thebaseline_fit` object.


Code
lm_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

lm_recipe <- recipe(sleep_duration ~ ., data = train_data) |>
  step_rm(age_group) |> 
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

lm_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lm_spec) |>
  add_recipe(lm_recipe)

baseline_fit <- fit(lm_workflow, data = train_data)

text:
Q2.4 Exploring ways to improve the model
To improve on the baseline linear regression model, an Elastic Net regression is implemented.






Note



Elastic Net is a regularised model that combines both Lasso and Ridge penalties, allowing it to perform variable selection while reducing multicollinearity and overfitting. This approach is particularly suitable for this dataset, as several predictors exhibit non-normal distributions and strong pairwise correlations.


To prepare the data appropriately for regularised modelling, the recipe applies dummy encoding to categorical variables, removes the manually constructed age_group variable to avoid redundancy, and uses the Yeo–Johnson transformation followed by normalisation to stabilise variance and place all predictors on a comparable scale. The penalty and mixture hyperparameters are tuned using 10-fold cross-validation with stratification on the outcome variable to maintain balanced folds. The best-performing parameter combination (based on RMSE) is then selected and used to fit the final Elastic Net model.


Code
enet_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")

enet_recipe <- recipe(sleep_duration ~ ., data = train_data) |>
  step_rm(age_group) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_YeoJohnson(all_numeric_predictors()) |>　# important!
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

enet_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_model(enet_spec) |>
  add_recipe(enet_recipe)

set.seed(234) 
train_folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 10, strata = sleep_duration)

set.seed(345)
enet_tune_results <- tune_grid(
  enet_workflow,
  resamples = train_folds, 
  grid = 20                
)

collect_metrics(enet_tune_results) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  arrange(mean)

The Elastic Net tuning procedure produced a model with a very small penalty (0.000207) and a mixture value of 1, meaning that the optimal model effectively collapses to a pure Lasso regression. The cross-validation results show that a wide range of mixture values produced nearly identical RMSE values (0.259), suggesting that the model is relatively insensitive to the balance between L1 and L2 penalties. The selection of mixture = 1 therefore reflects a slight advantage for sparsity rather than a structural dependence on ridge-style regularisation.

section: Q3.1 Splitting the data into training and test sets
text:
Q3.1 Splitting the data into training and test sets
To begin the classification task, the continuous outcome sleep_duration must be converted into a binary variable indicating whether a participant achieves adequate or inadequate sleep. Following common recommendations in sleep research, a threshold of 7 hours per night is used to define adequate sleep. A new factor variable, adequate_sleep, is therefore created, coded as “adequate” for durations ≥ 7 hours and “inadequate” otherwise.






Stratified Sampling



As in the regression analysis in Part 2, the data is split into training (75%) and test (25%) sets using stratified sampling. Here, stratification is applied to the new binary sleep outcome to maintain a similar proportion of adequate and inadequate sleepers in both subsets, ensuring a fair and reliable foundation for the classification models that follow.




Code
sleep_class <- sleep_clean |>
  mutate(
    adequate_sleep = if_else(
      sleep_duration >= 7,
      "adequate",
      "inadequate"
    ) |> factor(levels = c("inadequate", "adequate"))
  )

set.seed(456)

class_split <- initial_split(
  sleep_class,
  prop   = 0.75,
  strata = adequate_sleep  
)

train_class <- training(class_split)
test_class  <- testing(class_split)

Importantly, the class distribution is well preserved in the test set, with 55 adequate sleepers and 39 inadequate sleepers, closely reflecting the proportions in the full dataset, which reduces the risk of biased model training or misleading performance estimates.

title: DS202A - W08 Summative
section: Q3.2 Fitting a baseline logistic regression classifier
text:
Q3.2 Fitting a baseline logistic regression classifier
Diverging from the comprehensive approach used in the regression analysis, a parsimonious strategy was adopted for the baseline classifier to ensure numerical stability. Preliminary diagnostics indicated that including quality_of_sleep caused complete separation; thus, it was excluded to prevent unstable coefficient estimates. Consequently, the baseline model was restricted to stress_level and age, establishing a clear, interpretable benchmark and minimizing overfitting given the limited sample size.






Variable Selection



stress_level and age were selected based on both statistical evidence and practical interpretability. Exploratory analysis (Part 1) identified stress_level as the strongest predictor of sleep_duration (r=−0.81) after excluding sleep_quality, while age showed a moderate but distinct positive association (r=0.34). By combining a modifiable lifestyle factor (stress) with a fixed demographic attribute (age), this baseline model captures two fundamental dimensions of sleep behavior while minimizing multicollinearity issues often found with physiological metrics like heart_rate.




Code
log_spec_baseline <- logistic_reg() |> 
  set_engine("glm")

log_recipe_baseline <- recipe(
  adequate_sleep ~ stress_level + age,  
  data = train_class
) |> 
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

log_workflow_baseline <- workflow() |> 
  add_model(log_spec_baseline) |> 
  add_recipe(log_recipe_baseline)

log_fit_baseline <- fit(log_workflow_baseline, data = train_class)

tidy(log_fit_baseline)

The baseline logistic regression reveals highly significant associations for both predictors (p<0.001). Specifically, stress_level exhibits a strong negative coefficient (−2.92), indicating that as stress increases, the likelihood of achieving adequate sleep diminishes substantially. Similarly, age shows a negative association (-1.19), suggesting that older participants are statistically less likely to meet the adequate sleep threshold, holding stress levels constant.






Age Coefficient



A notable finding in this baseline model is the negative coefficient for Age (−1.19), which contradicts the positive correlation observed in the exploratory analysis and linear regression. The logistic regression suggests that, when holding stress_level constant, older participants are less likely to cross the specific threshold of 7 hours defined for “adequate” sleep. This discrepancy may arise from the specific distribution of sleep_duration around the cutoff point or potential interactions between age and stress. For instance, while older adults might sleep longer on average, they may cluster just below the 7-hour threshold or have a different relationship with stress compared to younger cohorts, leading to a reversal in the conditional probability of adequacy.

title: DS202A - W08 Summative
section: Q3.4 Exploring ways to improve the classifier
text:
Q3.4 Exploring ways to improve the classifier
A more sophisticated modeling approach is explored to maximize predictive performance. While the baseline logistic regression provided interpretability, it relies on linear assumptions that may oversimplify complex lifestyle interactions(e.g., physical activity × stress). To address this, a Random Forest classifier is introduced.






Model Selection Summary



A Random Forest classifier was chosen as the improved model because

it naturally handles nonlinear relationships
it is robust to multicollinearity
it allows the inclusion of all predictors without risking complete separation.





Code
rf_spec <- rand_forest(
  mtry = tune(),
  trees = 500,
  min_n = tune()
) |> 
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |> 
  set_mode("classification")

rf_recipe <- recipe(
  adequate_sleep ~ ., 
  data = train_class
) |> 
  step_rm(sleep_duration) |> 
  step_rm(quality_of_sleep) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) 

rf_workflow <- workflow() |> 
  add_model(rf_spec) |> 
  add_recipe(rf_recipe)

set.seed(789)
cv_folds_class <- vfold_cv(train_class, v = 10, strata = adequate_sleep)

rf_grid <- grid_regular(
  mtry(range = c(2, 10)),
  min_n(range = c(2, 20)),
  levels = 5
)

rf_tune_res <- tune_grid(
  rf_workflow,
  resamples = cv_folds_class,
  grid = rf_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy)
)

best_rf <- select_best(rf_tune_res, metric = "roc_auc")

final_rf_workflow <- finalize_workflow(rf_workflow, best_rf)
final_rf_fit <- last_fit(final_rf_workflow, class_split)

collect_metrics(final_rf_fit)

title: DS202A - W08 Summative
text:
Q3.5 Interpretation
The comparison between the baseline logistic regression and the Random Forest classifier provides decisive insights into the determinants of sleep adequacy. The Random Forest model achieved near-perfect predictive performance, indicating that when non-linear interactions and the full spectrum of lifestyle variables are accounted for, the distinction between adequate and inadequate sleepers becomes almost deterministic within this dataset.
Analysis of the Variable Importance Plot reveals a clear hierarchy of influence. Both stress_level and physical_activity_level emerged as the most critical drivers of sleep outcomes, reinforcing the conclusion that sleep adequacy is governed by a dual mechanism of psychological state and physiological activity. Notably, age ranked sixth in importance within the non-linear model. This lower ranking, combined with the model’s superior performance, helps resolve the paradoxical negative coefficient observed in the linear baseline (Q3.2). It suggests that age itself is less of a direct determinant and more of a confounding factor, whose influence is better explained by its complex interactions with activity levels and stress, which the Random Forest successfully disentangled.
These findings offer actionable strategies for public health and individual sleep management. The dominance of stress_level and physical_activity_level suggests that interventions should prioritize a holistic approach: promoting active lifestyles while simultaneously implementing stress-reduction techniques. Targeting these two modifiable levers is likely to be the most effective strategy for improving sleep duration across the population.

title: DS202A - W08 Summative
section: Q4.1 Ethical considerations of predicting sleep outcomes from lifestyle data
text:
Q4.1 Ethical considerations of predicting sleep outcomes from lifestyle data
Several ethical concerns arise when building predictive models using lifestyle and health-related data. First, such data are inherently sensitive, meaning that participants may face privacy risks if information about stress levels, heart rate, or sleep patterns is misused or inadequately protected. Because lifestyle indicators can be linked to mental or physical health, improper handling may lead to stigmatization or discrimination. For example, by employers or insurers inferring reduced productivity or increased risk. Second, predictions about “adequate sleep” could be interpreted as normative judgments about personal habits, potentially reinforcing harmful stereotypes about age, gender, occupation, or socioeconomic status. Third, algorithmic predictions may influence behaviour: individuals who receive unfavourable classifications might experience anxiety or adopt counterproductive health behaviours. Therefore, sleep-prediction models should be developed and deployed with a clear commitment to privacy, informed consent, and respect for individual autonomy, ensuring that predictions are used to support well-being rather than surveillance or evaluation.

title: DS202A - W08 Summative
section: Q4.2 Potential sources of bias or confounding
text:
Q4.2 Potential sources of bias or confounding
Predictive modelling in this context is vulnerable to several forms of bias and confounding. For example, stress_level is strongly associated with both sleep_duration and many unobserved factors such as work demands, caregiving responsibilities, or socioeconomic disadvantage. Without proper adjustment, the model may attribute differences in sleep adequacy to lifestyle choices when they are partly driven by structural or environmental conditions. Similarly, variables such as physical_activity_level or daily_steps may act as proxies for access to safe outdoor spaces, free time, or general health status, embedding social inequalities into model predictions. Sampling bias is also a concern: if participants in the dataset are healthier, younger, or more technologically engaged than the general population, the model’s performance will not generalise well. Measurement confounding is another issue. Self-reported sleep quality or stress may reflect personality traits rather than objective conditions, potentially distorting relationships between predictors and outcomes. These sources of bias highlight the need for cautious interpretation and underscore that statistical associations do not necessarily imply direct causal effects.

title: DS202A - W08 Summative
section: Q4.3 Additional variables or modelling approaches that could strengthen predictions
text:
Q4.3 Additional variables or modelling approaches that could strengthen predictions
Predictive performance could be enhanced by incorporating additional variables that capture structural and behavioural influences on sleep. Environmental factors such as noise exposure, work hours, shift patterns, commuting time, bedroom light levels, or access to green spaces may provide substantial explanatory power. Data on mental health (e.g., anxiety or depression scores), medication use, alcohol consumption, and digital-device screen time are also strongly linked to sleep behaviour and would likely improve classification accuracy. From a methodological perspective, more flexible models such as gradient-boosted trees or Bayesian additive regression trees could capture complex nonlinear structures and interactions that are difficult to model using logistic regression alone. Time-series or longitudinal modelling would allow sleep patterns to be understood as dynamic processes rather than static snapshots. Finally, causal-inference frameworks such as propensity-score methods or structural equation modelling could help separate predictive associations from underlying mechanisms, providing richer insight into how lifestyle factors influence sleep.

title: DS202A - W08 Summative
section: Q4.4 Communicating findings responsibly to a non-technical audience
text:
Q4.4 Communicating findings responsibly to a non-technical audience
Communicating sleep-prediction findings to non-technical audiences requires an emphasis on clarity, humility, and responsible interpretation. Technical details such as model architecture or tuning should be simplified into intuitive explanations.

“The model looks for patterns across lifestyle factors to estimate the likelihood of achieving sufficient sleep.”

It is crucial to distinguish correlations from causation and explicitly state that the model identifies statistical associations, not deterministic rules. Uncertainty should be highlighted by explaining that predictions may be inaccurate for some individuals and should not be used as medical diagnoses or performance evaluations. To avoid reinforcing stereotypes, model outputs should be framed in terms of general tendencies rather than inherent characteristics of specific groups. Most importantly, communication should focus on actionable, supportive insights.

“Higher stress levels were consistently associated with shorter sleep in this dataset.”

rather than

“People with high stress do not sleep adequately”.

By foregrounding transparency and empowerment, the findings can be communicated in a way that promotes understanding without overstating the model’s capabilities.
